{{< include _poly-kit.qmd >}}

**Math rock** is a style of rock from the late 1980s and 1990s on, built on odd meters, changing meters,
and riffs that run against the beat. Much of what sounds like "polyrhythm" in it is **polymeter**: riffs of
different lengths on the same pulse.

## A riff in five over four

The guitar repeats a five-step riff while the drums keep a four-step bar. Every step is the same length, so
the riff starts one step earlier in each new bar, and the two meet again after 20 steps.

<div class="poly" data-layers="X.x.x;X.x.;x" data-names="Guitar riff (5);Kick and snare (4);Hi-hat" data-sounds="hi;kick;shaker" data-bpm="90" data-beat="1" data-polymeter></div>

**Try it.** Mute the guitar and play the riff on your instrument (any five-note figure works) while the drums
play. Count "1 2 3 4 5" for the riff and feel the drums' "1 2 3 4" at the same time.

## Seven over four

<div class="poly" data-layers="X.x.xx.;X.x.;x" data-names="Riff (7);Kick and snare (4);Hi-hat" data-sounds="hi;kick;shaker" data-bpm="90" data-beat="1" data-polymeter></div>

Seven and four meet after 28 steps. Long cycles like this sound unpredictable but are fully fixed.

## Two guitars in two cycles

A trick heard in math rock and in progressive rock before it: two guitars play riffs of different lengths at the
same time. Here one guitar is in 5 and the other in 6, over drums in 4.

<div class="poly" data-layers="X.xx.;X..x.x;X.x." data-names="Guitar 1 (5);Guitar 2 (6);Drums (4)" data-sounds="hi;mid;kick" data-bpm="80" data-beat="2" data-polymeter></div>

All three line up after 60 steps. Mute layers to hear each pair.

## True polyrhythm: 3 and 5 against 4

Math rock also uses even polyrhythms, for example a guitar playing five even notes over a drummer's
four beats, both starting together each bar.

<div class="poly" data-layers="4;5;3" data-names="Four beats;Five;Three" data-sounds="kick;hi;wood" data-bpm="70" data-beat="0"></div>

The difference from the riffs above: here every layer starts again on each bar. In polymeter, the layers drift
and meet only after many bars.

## Bands to hear

From memory, as a listening list rather than checked claims about particular songs: Don Caballero, Hella,
Battles, Tera Melos, toe and Covet. King Crimson's early-1980s albums (*Discipline*) are often cited for two
guitars in different cycles, and Meshuggah, a metal band, for long riffs over a steady 4/4 hi-hat.

## Write your own

In the [Polyrhythm tool](../tools/polyrhythm.qmd), tick **Polymeter**, keep a 4-step drum layer, and type a riff
of 3, 5, 7 or 9 steps. Then add a second riff of another length. The line under the grid tells you when they
all line up again: that is the length of your section.

Back to the start: [What Is a Polyrhythm?](poly-basics.qmd)
